title: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and advanced hunting
summary: Tour the full Defender for Endpoint platform — next-gen AV, EDR, attack surface reduction and threat & vulnerability management — then learn to query its raw telemetry with KQL advanced hunting and turn a query into a custom detection rule.
objectives: Describe the core Defender for Endpoint capabilities: next-gen AV, EDR, ASR rules, network protection and TVM
Compare onboarding methods and explain what telemetry an onboarded device emits
Navigate the advanced hunting data model and identify the key Device* schema tables
Write KQL using where, project, summarize, parse and join across DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceNetworkEvents and DeviceLogonEvents
Promote a validated hunting query into a custom detection rule and map findings to MITRE ATT&CK
Use the device timeline and live response for hands-on investigation and remediation

quiz.q: Which Defender for Endpoint capability proactively reduces the available attack surface by blocking risky behaviours such as Office apps spawning child processes?
quiz.why: ASR rules are configurable controls that block or audit risky behaviours (Office child processes, obfuscated scripts, credential theft from LSASS), shrinking the attack surface before an exploit can run.

quiz.q: In advanced hunting, which KQL operator is correct for selecting only the columns you want to keep in the result set?
quiz.why: project chooses and reshapes the columns returned; where filters rows. KQL has no select keyword, and parse/extract pull substrings out of a single field.

quiz.q: You want to correlate a suspicious process with the network connections it made. Which two schema tables and join key are most appropriate?
options: DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents joined on DeviceId and InitiatingProcessId
quiz.why: Process-to-network correlation joins DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents; the network table records the InitiatingProcess* fields, so you match on DeviceId plus the initiating process identity to tie a connection back to its parent process.

quiz.q: What is the effect of promoting a validated advanced hunting query into a custom detection rule?
options: It deletes the underlying telemetry to save storage
It runs the query on a schedule and generates alerts plus optional automated response actions
It exports the query to a CSV once and stops
It disables the built-in Microsoft detections
quiz.why: A custom detection rule runs your KQL on a recurring frequency, raises an alert when rows return, and can trigger response actions such as isolating the device or collecting an investigation package.

quiz.q: Name the advanced hunting schema table you would query to investigate interactive and remote sign-in activity on a device, and one field you would use to spot anomalous logons.
quiz.answer: DeviceLogonEvents. Useful fields include LogonType (for example Interactive, Network, RemoteInteractive), AccountName, RemoteIP and ActionType (LogonSuccess or LogonFailed) to spot brute force or unusual remote logons.
quiz.why: DeviceLogonEvents records authentication on the device; LogonType plus failed/success ActionType and source RemoteIP reveal lateral movement, password spraying and unexpected RemoteInteractive (RDP) sessions.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain why mapping a hunting finding to MITRE ATT&CK is valuable during an investigation.
quiz.answer: Mapping to ATT&CK tactics and techniques gives the behaviour a shared, standard name so you can communicate it clearly, find related detections, anticipate the attacker's next likely step and measure your coverage gaps.
quiz.why: ATT&CK provides a common taxonomy of adversary tactics and techniques; framing findings against it turns isolated observations into an understandable kill-chain and drives consistent, comparable detection engineering.

body_markdown:
## What Defender for Endpoint actually is

**Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE)** is not a single antivirus product; it is a layered endpoint protection platform. The layers worth knowing: **next-generation antivirus** (cloud-backed, behaviour-based protection), **endpoint detection and response (EDR)** that records rich behavioural telemetry and raises alerts, **attack surface reduction (ASR) rules** that block risky behaviours like an Office app spawning a child process, **network protection** that blocks connections to malicious domains and IPs, and **threat & vulnerability management (TVM)** that inventories software and surfaces exploitable CVEs with remediation guidance.

The layer that makes MDE a hunting platform is EDR: every onboarded device continuously streams **behavioural telemetry** — process creations, network connections, file writes, logons, registry edits — into the cloud where you can query it.

## Onboarding and the data it produces

A device only contributes telemetry once it is **onboarded**. Common methods: **Intune** (the modern default for managed Windows), **Group Policy** or a local **onboarding script**, **Microsoft Configuration Manager**, and platform-native onboarding for macOS and Linux. Onboarding installs the sensor and connects the device to your tenant. From that moment its events flow into the **advanced hunting** schema.

## The advanced hunting data model

**Advanced hunting** is a query-based investigation tool over up to 30 days of raw event data, written in **KQL** (Kusto Query Language). The schema is organised into tables; the endpoint ones are prefixed `Device`:

- `DeviceProcessEvents` — process creations and command lines.
- `DeviceNetworkEvents` — outbound and inbound connections.
- `DeviceFileEvents` — file create, modify, rename, delete.
- `DeviceLogonEvents` — interactive, network and remote logons.
- `DeviceRegistryEvents`, `DeviceImageLoadEvents`, `DeviceEvents` — registry, DLL loads and miscellaneous sensor events.

Every row carries `DeviceId`, `Timestamp` and a set of `InitiatingProcess*` columns describing the parent process — these are the keys you join on.

## Writing KQL over the schema

KQL reads top to bottom, piping a table through operators. The core verbs are **where** (filter rows), **project** (choose columns), **summarize** (aggregate), **parse** (extract from a string) and **join** (correlate tables). Hunt for a script interpreter launched from Office:

```kql
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe", "excel.exe", "outlook.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "cmd.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
```

Now correlate suspicious processes with the connections they made by **joining** the process and network tables on the device and initiating process:

```kql
let suspect = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-enc", "DownloadString", "FromBase64String");
suspect
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
) on DeviceId, $left.ProcessId == $right.InitiatingProcessId
| summarize Connections = count() by DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Connections desc
```

## From query to detection and investigation

A query that reliably finds bad behaviour should not stay manual. Use **Create detection rule** to schedule the KQL, raise an alert when rows return, and optionally trigger response actions. Each alert is mapped to **MITRE ATT&CK** tactics and techniques so the behaviour gets a shared name and a place in the kill chain.

For hands-on work, the **device timeline** shows a chronological event stream, and **live response** gives you a secure remote shell:

```text
live response session (analyst):
  connect <deviceId>
  getfile "C:\Users\Public\dropper.ps1"   # collect evidence
  processes                                  # list running processes
  remediate file <SHA1>                      # quarantine
  run TriageScript.ps1                        # run a library script
```

Isolation, package collection and file quarantine can all be driven from here or automated by the detection rule.

## Your task

In a test tenant's advanced hunting, write a query that hunts for likely lateral movement: find `DeviceLogonEvents` with `LogonType == "RemoteInteractive"` (RDP) where the same `RemoteIP` produced more than five `LogonFailed` events before a `LogonSuccess` within an hour. Use `summarize` with `count()` and time bucketing, `project` only the fields an analyst needs, then join back to `DeviceProcessEvents` to show what the successful session ran. Finally, describe how you would promote it to a custom detection rule and which ATT&CK technique it maps to.

slides.narration: Welcome back to Month Three. In the last lessons we set the Zero Trust foundation; now we get hands-on with the platform that gives us the telemetry behind it. This lesson is Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and advanced hunting. By the end you'll understand every layer of the platform, and you'll be writing K Q L queries against raw endpoint data to hunt threats yourself.

slides.title: More than antivirus
bullets: MDE is a layered platform, not a single AV.
Next-gen AV, EDR, ASR rules, network protection, TVM.
EDR streams rich behavioural telemetry to the cloud.
That telemetry is what you'll hunt over.
slides.narration: First, let's dispel a myth. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is not just an antivirus. It's a layered platform. You get next-generation antivirus that's cloud-backed and behaviour-based. You get E D R, endpoint detection and response, which records rich behavioural telemetry and raises alerts. You get attack surface reduction rules, network protection, and threat and vulnerability management. The layer that turns it into a hunting platform is E D R, because every onboarded device streams its behaviour into the cloud for you to query.

slides.title: Attack surface reduction
bullets: ASR rules block risky behaviours before exploit.
Example: stop Office apps spawning child processes.
Block credential theft from LSASS, obfuscated scripts.
Run in audit first, then flip to block.
slides.narration: Let's single out attack surface reduction, because it's one of the highest-value controls you can deploy. A S R rules block known-risky behaviours proactively. Classic examples: stop Microsoft Office applications from spawning child processes, block credential theft from the L S A S S process, block obfuscated scripts. The smart way to roll these out is in audit mode first, watch what they would have blocked using advanced hunting, and only then flip them to block so you don't break a legitimate workflow.

slides.title: Onboarding produces telemetry
bullets: A device only emits data once onboarded.
Methods: Intune, Group Policy, script, ConfigMgr.
Onboarding installs the sensor, links to your tenant.
macOS and Linux have native onboarding too.
slides.narration: Telemetry only exists once a device is onboarded. There are several ways to do it: Intune is the modern default for managed Windows, but you can also use Group Policy, a local onboarding script, or Configuration Manager. macOS and Linux have their own native onboarding paths. Whatever the method, onboarding installs the sensor and connects the device to your tenant. From that moment, its process, network, file and logon events start flowing into the advanced hunting schema.

slides.title: The advanced hunting data model
bullets: Query up to 30 days of raw events with KQL.
Endpoint tables are prefixed Device.
Process, Network, File, Logon, Registry events.
Every row has DeviceId, Timestamp, InitiatingProcess fields.
slides.narration: Advanced hunting is a query tool over up to thirty days of raw event data, and you write those queries in K Q L, the Kusto Query Language. The data is organised into tables, and the endpoint ones all start with the word Device. Device Process Events, Device Network Events, Device File Events, Device Logon Events, and more for registry and loaded images. The important thing: every single row carries a Device I D, a timestamp, and a set of initiating-process fields describing the parent. Those are the columns you'll join on.

slides.title: KQL core verbs
bullets: where filters rows; project picks columns.
summarize aggregates; parse extracts from strings.
join correlates two tables together.
Data flows top to bottom through the pipe.
slides.code:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe", "excel.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "cmd.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
slides.narration: K Q L reads top to bottom, piping a table through each operator. Learn five verbs and you can hunt. Where filters rows. Project chooses which columns to keep. Summarize aggregates, like counting. Parse pulls a value out of a text field. And join correlates two tables. Here's a real hunt: start from Device Process Events, filter to the last seven days, find cases where Word or Excel launched PowerShell or command prompt, then project just the fields that matter. That's a classic suspicious-Office-child-process query.

slides.title: Joining process and network
bullets: A let statement names a reusable sub-query.
Join DeviceProcessEvents to DeviceNetworkEvents.
Match on DeviceId and the initiating process id.
summarize the connections each command made.
slides.code:
let suspect = DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName =~ "powershell.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-enc", "DownloadString");
suspect
| join kind=inner (DeviceNetworkEvents) on DeviceId,
    $left.ProcessId == $right.InitiatingProcessId
| summarize count() by DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
slides.narration: Now the powerful move: correlation. A let statement names a reusable sub-query — here, suspicious PowerShell with encoded commands or download cradles. Then we join that to Device Network Events. We match on the Device I D and on the process identity, because the network table records the initiating process that opened each connection. Finally we summarize how many connections each command line made, to which U R Ls and I Ps. In one query we've tied a suspicious process to its command-and-control traffic.

slides.title: Query to detection rule
bullets: A reliable query shouldn't stay manual.
Create detection rule runs it on a schedule.
It raises alerts and can trigger response actions.
Each alert maps to MITRE ATT&CK tactics.
slides.narration: Once a query reliably finds bad behaviour, don't keep running it by hand. Use Create detection rule. That schedules your K Q L to run on a recurring frequency, raises an alert whenever rows come back, and can optionally trigger automated responses like isolating the device or collecting an investigation package. And every alert it raises is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques, so the behaviour gets a shared, standard name and slots into the kill chain. That's how a hunt becomes durable detection engineering.

slides.title: Timeline and live response
bullets: Device timeline shows events chronologically.
Live response is a secure remote shell.
Collect files, list processes, quarantine, run scripts.
Isolate the device when you need to contain.
slides.code:
connect <deviceId>
getfile "C:\Users\Public\dropper.ps1"
processes
remediate file <SHA1>
run TriageScript.ps1
slides.narration: For hands-on investigation you have two great tools. The device timeline gives you a chronological stream of everything that happened on a machine — perfect for reconstructing an incident. And live response gives you a secure remote shell straight into the endpoint. From there you can collect a suspicious file as evidence, list running processes, quarantine a file by its hash, or run a triage script from your library. And when you need to contain, you can isolate the device from the network with a single action.

bullets: MDE layers: next-gen AV, EDR, ASR, network, TVM.
Hunt raw telemetry with KQL over the Device tables.

slides.narration: Let's recap. Defender for Endpoint is a layered platform — next-gen antivirus, E D R, attack surface reduction, network protection and vulnerability management. Its E D R telemetry lands in the advanced hunting schema, which you query with K Q L over the Device tables, joining process, network and logon events to correlate behaviour. Your task: in a test tenant, write a hunting query for likely lateral movement. Find remote interactive R D P logons where the same remote I P had more than five failed logons before a success within an hour, summarize and project cleanly, then join back to Device Process Events to show what that session ran. Describe how you'd promote it to a custom detection rule and which ATT&CK technique it maps to. See you in the next lesson.
